lesson.menu_title: The Renewal That Almost Did Not Happen
lesson.menu_desc: Reading an account review and telling the story of a near-loss: what has been happening since March, and what has been done about it -- present perfect continuous
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 24 -- The Renewal That Almost Did Not Happen: the story of a near-loss

lesson.grammar_point: present perfect continuous (has been / have been + -ing)

reading.rtitle: Account Review — Northwind Logistics · Renewal: June 30
paras: Northwind Logistics has been a customer for four years, and until March it was one of the healthiest accounts in the region. Since the ticket sync outage in March, the picture has changed. Usage has been falling for three months: two of the five teams have stopped opening the dashboard completely, and the number of active users has gone down from four hundred to two hundred and sixty. Engagement is low as well. David, our main point of contact, has not answered the last two invitations to the monthly call, and nobody from his team joined the training we ran in May. The renewal date is June the thirtieth, so there are eight weeks left.

Three red flags are on this account. First, the finance team at Northwind has been asking for a full comparison of the market since April, and another vendor presented to David's director last Thursday. Second, our executive sponsor inside Northwind changed in February, and the new one has never seen a business review from us, so there is no buy-in above David. Third, the adoption plan has been stalling since the outage: the two workshops that were agreed in the last review have not been delivered, because the dates have been moved three times. None of these three is fatal on its own. Together, they say that the account is at risk.

The plan for the next eight weeks has three parts. We have been running weekly sessions with the two inactive teams since the beginning of May, and their usage has already gone up by eleven per cent. We are preparing a business review for the new sponsor, with the numbers of the last four years and not only of the last four months. And David has asked for one page that he can take to his director: what has been done since the outage, what has been changed, and what the next twelve months look like. A turnaround here is possible, but it is a turnaround and not a formality: this renewal has to be won back, not signed.
reading.source: Adapted for class use from a customer success account review

gist.prompt: What is the best one-line summary of this account review?
choices: It is a complaint about the March outage and about who caused it.
It says why a four-year account is now at risk, what the warning signs have been, and what is being done to win it back.
It is a price proposal for the renewal in June.

items: Usage on this account has been falling since before the March outage.
Until March it was one of the healthiest accounts in the region; usage has been falling for three months, since the outage.
The new executive sponsor at Northwind has already seen a business review from us.
The new one has never seen a business review from us, so there is no buy-in above David.
The two workshops agreed in the last review have not been delivered.
The adoption plan has been stalling since the outage, because the dates have been moved three times.
The weekly sessions with the two inactive teams have already produced a result.
Their usage has already gone up by eleven per cent.
This review names three red flags, and not one of them is about price. In your own accounts, which red flag do you usually see first?
David has not answered the last two invitations to the monthly call. When is silence from a customer a warning sign, and when is it only a busy month?
If you had one page for David's director, which three numbers would you put on it, and why those three?

listenings.text: Hi Patrícia, this is David. I am leaving this note because I do not want you to hear it from somebody else. Our contract comes up for renewal on the thirtieth of June, and the finance team here has been asking me hard questions since April. They have been talking to another vendor for about six weeks now, and last Thursday that vendor presented to my director. I am not telling you this to put pressure on you. I am telling you because I have been defending this platform inside my own company for two years, and at the moment I am running out of arguments. Two of my teams have not opened the dashboard since March, and when the numbers are that low, nobody in this building listens to me. So bring me something I can take to my director. Not a discount. Numbers, and a plan. Call me this week.

Hi Patrícia, it is Karen. I have been looking at the Northwind account all morning, and I want to say two things before your call with David. First, do not open with the outage. That story is closed: you reported it in March and you did it well. Open with what has been happening since then, because that is what his numbers show. Usage has been falling for three months and two teams have been off the dashboard since the release. Say it out loud before he does. A customer trusts the person who names the problem first. Second, when you talk about the work, say it as something that has not stopped. We have been running weekly sessions since May is a completely different sentence from we ran some sessions in May. The first one tells him the work is still going on today, and that is exactly what he needs to take to his director. And put a number next to every claim. You have three days. Let me know how it goes.
